events.title: DEC PDP-10 released
events.summary: Digital Equipment Corporation introduced the PDP-10 in 1966 — a 36-bit timesharing minicomputer that became a hub for early hacker culture.
events.about: The PDP-10 ran TOPS-10 and TOPS-20 — MIT, Stanford, and BBN used it for AI research, email, and the ARPANET. Emacs, Lisp machines, and countless hacker traditions started on PDP-10 systems. Its time-sharing model let dozens of users compile and debug simultaneously — the environment that shaped Unix's design at Bell Labs.

narrative.whyChosen: The PDP-10 was the dominant timesharing machine of the 1960s–70s research community.
narrative.whyImportant: It hosted the communities and tools that defined interactive computing and early networking.
narrative.problemSolved: Research labs needed shared interactive access to a powerful computer, not batch punch-card queues.

events.title: Joseph Weizenbaum creates ELIZA
events.summary: Joseph Weizenbaum created ELIZA at MIT in 1966 — a program that simulated conversation by pattern-matching user text, including the DOCTOR Rogerian therapist script.
events.about: ELIZA fooled some users into attributing understanding to a simple keyword engine — prompting Weizenbaum's later warnings about anthropomorphizing machines. It launched chatbot research and debates about AI deception that continue in modern LLM guardrails.

narrative.whyChosen: ELIZA was the first widely known conversational computer program.
narrative.whyImportant: It showed how little code could mimic dialogue — and why users over-trust machines.
narrative.problemSolved: Researchers wanted to explore natural-language interaction without real language understanding.
